P0100.d: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency.
s: Rough idle, hesitation, lack of power (substitute value)
c: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or supply wire open
Sensor faulty internally (broken element, failed electronics)

P0101.d: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency.
s: Check engine light on, often without driveability problems
Hesitation, flat spot, poor throttle response
Higher consumption, often with lean codes P0171/P0174
c: Air leak between sensor and engine (cracked or loose intake duct, boost leak)
Contaminated sensing element (oil from oiled sport filter, dust)
Clogged or wrongly fitted air filter, modified intake
Aged sensor or poor contact in the wiring

s: Lack of power, hesitation, substitute value mode
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground, connector corroded or loose
Missing supply voltage (fuse, relay) or poor ground
Large leak or disconnected duct between sensor and throttle

c: Signal wire shorted to voltage or to the supply wire

Water in the connector or on the element

Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency.
s: Check engine light on, may go out again
Occasional hesitation, misfire-like stumble, flat spot
c: Loose contact at the sensor connector (corrosion, spread terminals, broken latch)
Chafed or partly broken wire moved by the engine

P0105.d: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.
s: Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit (diesel)
Rough idle, hard starting, higher consumption (petrol)
c: Connector or wiring to the sensor open, shorted or loose
MAP sensor faulty (oiled, failed internally, SENT status fault)
Sensor hose disconnected, vacuum or boost leak
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor on the same circuit

P0106.d: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.
s: Higher consumption, black smoke possible on diesels
Loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines
c: Vacuum leak at the intake manifold or boost leak (hose, clamp, charge air cooler)
Sensor oiled or sooted, port blocked (EGR soot), characteristic drifted
High resistance in signal, reference or ground wire
Comparison sensor wrong, or mechanical cause (dirty throttle, EGR stuck open)

P0107.d: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.
s: Hard starting, rough idle, stalling possible
Wrong mixture from substitute value, higher consumption
Loss of power or limp mode on turbo and diesel engines
c: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or reference wire open
5 V reference shorted by another faulty sensor on the same circuit

It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.
s: Rough idle, loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines
c: Ground (low reference) wire open or connector corroded
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage

It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.
s: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)
c: Loose contact at the MAP connector, terminals spread or corroded
Chafed or broken wire that makes contact with engine movement

P010A.d: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010A is the general circuit fault of sensor B: no usable signal at all, just like P0100 for sensor A.
c: Connector or wiring of sensor B open
Supply of sensor B missing (fuse, relay)

P010B.d: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010B is the plausibility fault of sensor B: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit.
c: Intake pipe on the sensor B side leaking or not seated
Air filter on that side clogged or wrongly fitted
Boost leak on that bank, or sensor/connector problem

P010C.d: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010C means the signal of sensor B is below its electrical lower limit – the counterpart of P0102.
s: Lack of power, substitute value mode
c: Signal wire of sensor B open or grounded, connector corroded
Supply or ground of sensor B faulty

P010D.d: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010D means the signal of sensor B is above its electrical upper limit – the counterpart of P0103.
s: Substitute value mode, lack of power
Rich mixture and higher consumption possible
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to voltage

P010E.d: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010E covers brief dropouts or jumps in the signal of sensor B without a lasting low or high fault, the counterpart of P0104.
s: Check engine light on, may come and go
c: Loose contact at the sensor B connector

P010F.d: Engines with two intake paths have two mass air flow sensors, A and B. On a symmetrical V engine both sides should draw about the same amount of air, so the readings can be compared with each other.
s: Mixture codes for one bank (P0171/P0174) possible
c: Air leak or loose intake pipe on one side
One of the two sensors contaminated or aged
Air filter on one side clogged or wrongly fitted
Turbocharger or boost problem on one bank
Contact resistance in connector or wiring

P0110.d: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage.
s: Reduced power or torque limitation on some systems
Otherwise usually inconspicuous; cold start may be slightly worse
c: Connector or wiring to the sensor open or corroded
Sensor or mass air flow sensor with built-in temperature sensor faulty

P0111.d: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage.
s: Slightly changed idle, power or cold start possible
Code often returns only after an overnight soak
c: Sensor drifting or stuck at one value (ageing, oil from crankcase ventilation)
Contact resistance at connector or wiring distorts the reading
Comparison sensor (coolant, IAT2, charge air cooler) wrong
Undetected preheater, heat soak or sensor mounted near a heat source

s: Slightly richer mixture and higher consumption possible
c: Connector unplugged or loose, or wire broken
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

s: Occasional brief stumble or rough idle possible
c: Loose contact at the connector (corrosion, weak terminal tension)
Partly broken wire that opens with engine movement

P0115.d: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.
c: Connector corroded or loose, terminal spread
Broken or chafed signal or ground wire
Sensor faulty internally (short, open, coolant inside)
Control module input or 5 V supply faulty

Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.
c: Sensor drifting and reading too warm (ageing, coolant ingress)
Corrosion or contact resistance in connector or wiring
Block heater or preheater not detected

Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.
s: Hard cold start (no enrichment, engine reported hot)
c: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing, pinched harness)
Sensor shorted internally or coolant inside the sensor
Moisture or coolant in the connector

Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.
s: Rich mixture, higher consumption, possibly black smoke or fuel smell
c: Connector unplugged or corroded, contact open
Broken signal or sensor ground wire
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage

P0119.d: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.
s: Radiator fan switches on for no reason
Occasional rough running or idle fluctuation
c: Loose contact or corroded connector pins
Harness chafing that briefly grounds or opens with engine movement
Sensor with internal crack or contact fault
Air pockets at the sensor (poorly bled cooling system)

P011A.d: Some engines have two coolant temperature sensors that check each other. P011A is set when both are electrically fine but their readings differ more than a calibrated amount under conditions where they should agree.
c: Clogged heater core or restricted coolant flow at sensor 2
One of the two sensors drifting
Air in the cooling system or low coolant level

P011B.d: After a long standstill the coolant and the intake air should both have settled close to ambient temperature. P011B compares the two sensors at start-up and is set when they disagree without either sensor showing a circuit fault.
s: With a wrong coolant reading: poor cold start, higher consumption or odd fan behaviour
Code often returns only after an overnight soak
c: Coolant temperature sensor stuck or drifting
Intake air temperature sensor drifting or heat-soaked
Contact resistance at a sensor connector or ground
Control module software (false setting, update available)

P011C.d: On turbocharged engines a charge air cooler temperature sensor sits downstream of the compressor, usually after the charge air cooler, and intake air temperature sensor 1 sits upstream near the air filter. While driving they differ by design, because compression heats the air.
s: Code often returns only after an overnight soak
c: Charge air cooler temperature sensor drifting, oily or stuck
Contact resistance at connector or shared ground
Undetected preheating or uneven cooling (sun, residual heat)

P011D.d: This is the bank 2 counterpart of P011C and only exists on engines with two separate intake paths, each with its own charge air cooler temperature sensor and intake air temperature sensor – for example V engines with twin turbochargers and separate charge air coolers. After a long standstill both bank 2 sensors should read nearly the same; if they disagree at start-up, without either showing a circuit fault, P011D is
s: Code often returns only after an overnight soak
c: Bank 2 charge air cooler temperature sensor drifting, oily or stuck
Bank 2 intake air temperature sensor drifting
Contact resistance at connector or ground

P011E.d: After a long standstill, typically six to eight hours, the coolant should have cooled to roughly the outside air temperature measured by the ambient sensor in the bumper or mirror. P011E compares coolant temperature sensor 1 with the ambient sensor at start-up and is set when they differ beyond a calibrated limit and no preheater was detected.
c: Ambient temperature sensor drifting or affected by engine heat or sun
Contact resistance in one sensor's connector or wiring

P011F.d: This is the counterpart of P011E for the second coolant temperature sensor and only exists on engines that have one – for example at the engine outlet, the radiator or in the heater circuit. After a long standstill sensor 2 should also read roughly the outside temperature; if it disagrees with the ambient sensor beyond a calibrated limit at start-up, P011F is set without saying which sensor is wrong.
c: Ambient temperature sensor faulty or influenced

P0120.d: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).
s: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
c: Connector at the throttle body corroded or loose, broken wire
Sensor or throttle body with integrated sensor faulty
5 V reference disturbed (short on another sensor of the same circuit)

P0121.d: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).
s: Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
Shift problems on automatics (wrong load signal)
c: Carboned or mechanically sticking throttle plate
Worn potentiometer track (signal sticks or jumps)
Air leak or faulty MAF/MAP sensor (model comparison)
Contact resistance in signal or ground wire
Sensor or idle stop misadjusted (cable systems)

P0122.d: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).
s: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
Engine barely responds to the pedal or stalls at idle
High idle, A/C switched off (cable systems)
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
Connector at the throttle body loose or corroded
5 V reference missing (open, or shorted by another sensor)

P0123.d: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).
s: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
Raised idle or delayed throttle response
c: Sensor ground (low reference) open or high-resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or 12 V
Moisture or corrosion in the connector

P0124.d: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).
s: Check engine light, possibly only intermittently
Limp mode that disappears after restart
c: Loose contact in the connector (spread terminals, corrosion)
Chafed or partly broken wire in the harness
Worn potentiometer track (dropout at a certain position)

P0125.d: Closed-loop mixture control using the oxygen sensors is only released once the coolant has reached a minimum temperature. CARB requires that this happens within set times – from 2006 two minutes if the engine starts up to 8 °C below the release temperature, five minutes if 8–19 °C below.
s: Engine warms up slowly, heater stays cold for a long time
c: Thermostat stuck open (especially in cold weather)
Coolant sensor reading too cold or slow (drift, contact resistance)
Low coolant level or air at the sensor
Much idling or coasting in frost

P0126.d: The generic title refers to a coolant temperature that is not reached for stable operation, i.e. for releasing further functions and diagnostics; how manufacturers implement it differs.
s: Engine and heater warm up slowly
c: Coolant sensor frozen or faulty (resistance does not change)
Thermostat stuck open or low coolant
Contact resistance in connector or wiring

P0127.d: P0127 is not a circuit fault but a functional check of the air path: the measured intake air temperature is too high for the operating state. The logic is documented for a Bosch EDC16 diesel (Saab 9-3): if the intake air exceeds 130 °C and does not fall below it within 45 s after the exhaust gas recirculation valve is closed, hot exhaust gas is evidently still entering or the sensor is wrong.
s: Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit
Knock tendency and retarded ignition on petrol engines
c: EGR valve stuck open or not sealing (diesel)
EGR cooler clogged or bypass flap stuck in bypass
Charge air cooler dirty or airflow through it blocked
Sensor reading wrong, or hot engine-bay air drawn in (loose intake duct)

P0128.d: After a cold start the thermostat stays closed so the engine warms up quickly. CARB requires the coolant to reach a temperature at most 11 °C below the thermostat's rated value within a set time.
s: Temperature gauge stays low or drops while driving
Heater does not get properly warm
c: Thermostat stuck open or opening too early
Coolant sensor reading too low, or corrosion and resistance in its circuit
Low coolant level or air in the system
Radiator fan running constantly (relay stuck, wrong control)
Driving pattern or conditions (much idling, extreme cold, strong heating)

P0129.d: The engine control module needs the ambient air pressure for mixture, altitude correction and boost limits. It comes either from a dedicated barometric sensor or from the MAP sensor, read at key-on with the engine stopped and updated at wide-open throttle.
s: Rich mixture, higher consumption, rough idle
c: MAP or baro sensor reading too low (dirty, oiled, drifted)
High resistance or corrosion in signal wire or connector
Control module (baro sensor often built in) or software

P012A.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors.
c: Connector or wiring open, corroded or shorted
Sensor faulty (SENT sensor reports internal error)

P012B.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors.
s: Loss of power or boost limitation
c: Sensor oiled (crankcase vent often joins before the compressor) or drifted
Air filter heavily clogged or intake blocked or collapsed
Leak in the intake pipe between filter and compressor or at the sensor flange
Comparison sensor (MAP, baro, MAF) wrong or software

P012C.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors.
c: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or reference wire open
5 V reference shorted by another sensor

P012D.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors.
s: Reduced power or limp mode possible
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground open or connector corroded

P012E.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors.
s: Occasional power reduction or boost fluctuation
c: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector
Broken or chafed wire making intermittent contact

P012F.d: P012F compares the coolant temperature sensor with the engine oil temperature sensor. The documented user is Ford's Power Stroke diesel.
s: Check engine light and/or wrench lamp (Ford)
Raised oil temperature with a clogged oil cooler
Often no driving symptoms when software is the cause
c: Oil cooler (oil-to-coolant heat exchanger) clogged – oil much hotter than coolant
Engine module software (false setting, especially in cold weather)
Coolant or oil temperature sensor inaccurate, or its wiring faulty
Thermostat stuck open or low coolant
Block heater in use (only coolant preheated)

P0130.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip.
s: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure
Sensor and catalyst readiness not set
c: Wiring or connector of the bank 1 upstream sensor damaged, corroded or wet
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or mixture fault (plausibility versions)
Control module or sensor interface chip faulty

P0131.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip.
s: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure
c: Signal wire (or a wide-band sensor wire) shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on exhaust or gearbox
Sensor faulty or poisoned (permanently lean signal)
Large exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or misfires
Control module or interface chip faulty

P0132.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip.
s: Higher consumption, possibly soot or fuel smell
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure
Often with P0138 or heater codes
c: Signal wire shorted to the heater supply or battery voltage (melted or chafed harness)
Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire (GM reads its bias voltage)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Sensor contaminated by silicone, coolant or oil

P0133.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure
c: Aged, sooted or poisoned upstream sensor (oil, silicone, coolant, additives)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (manifold gasket, crack)
Sensor heater weak or intermittent (sensor too cold)
Mixture fault: air leak, injectors, fuel pressure, air flow sensor
Wiring resistance or aftermarket sensor with different characteristics

P0134.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip.
s: No mixture control (open loop), higher consumption
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure
c: Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire, connector loose or corroded
Sensor heater faulty – sensor does not get hot enough
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or cracked sensor
Control module bias or measuring circuit faulty

P0135.d: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1) has an electric heater so that it reaches its working temperature of about 300 °C soon after a cold start. The control module switches the heater on the ground side and checks driver voltage and heater current: GM fails it outside 0.3–2.5 A (or 3.1 A) and calls it 'heater performance', Ford outside roughly 0.22–0.465 A minimum to 3 A, Saab Trionic outside 0.5–2.3 A for
s: Longer cold-start phase without mixture control, more fuel and emissions
c: Heater element of the sensor burnt out (sensor must be replaced)
Fuse or relay of the heater supply faulty
Heater wiring or connector open, corroded or shorted
Heater driver in the control module faulty

P0136.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0136 is the general circuit code, and its exact meaning varies by manufacturer.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Slightly higher consumption possible without downstream trim
c: Downstream sensor aged or poisoned (stays in the middle band)
Signal or ground wire open or high-resistance, connector corroded
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor

P0137.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0137 means the signal stays below the lower limit.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Usually no noticeable change in driving
c: Signal wire shorted to ground or melted against the exhaust
Sensor faulty (cracked element, thermal shock from water)
Signal circuit open (counts as low on Ford)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (lean reading)
Signal and ground wires swapped after a repair

P0138.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0138 means the signal stays above the upper limit.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Usually no noticeable change in driving
c: Signal wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Signal circuit open or high-resistance (GM bias logic)
Genuinely rich exhaust or oil/coolant contamination

P0139.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0139 means the sensor reacts too slowly to mixture changes.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
c: Sensor aged or contaminated (oil ash, silicone, additives)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
Sensor heater weak, sensor too cold

P013A.d: The downstream oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) is used for fine mixture trim and to monitor the converter. 'Slow response' means the signal transition itself is too sluggish – it takes too long to pass between two voltage levels.
s: Usually no noticeable change in driving
Catalyst monitor may stay incomplete (inspection readiness missing)
With a converter cause, P0420/P0430 may follow
c: Downstream oxygen sensor aged or contaminated (soot, oil, silicone, coolant)
Exhaust leak between manifold/turbo and the sensor
Converter faulty or non-original with different oxygen storage
Control module software too sensitive (update available)
Sensor connector or wiring with contact resistance

P013B.d: The downstream oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) is used for fine mixture trim and to monitor the converter. 'Slow response' means the signal transition itself is too sluggish – it takes too long to pass between two voltage levels.
s: Usually no noticeable change in driving
Catalyst monitor may stay incomplete (inspection readiness missing)
With a converter cause, P0420/P0430 may follow

P01CB.d: Diesel engines must detect when fuel can no longer be injected at the correct crank angle – CARB requires this for every injector individually, hence one code per cylinder. The start of injection is not measured directly: during overrun with fuel cut-off the control module fires a tiny test injection into one cylinder (GM: about 1.5 mm³) and evaluates the resulting speed change at the crankshaft sensor.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
c: Injector worn, coked or sticking (opens late, delivers too little)
False setting from software or vehicle vibration (e.g. off-road tyres)
Wrong injector correction code stored after an injector replacement
Boost leak or loose injector clamp

P01E3.d: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. As with every NTC sensor, a low signal voltage means hot and a high one cold.
s: Coolant temperature or cooling fan behaviour possibly affected
